questions.prompt: Standard form of a linear program is
questions.explanation: Standard form minimizes a linear cost, forces every constraint to be an equality, and keeps every variable nonnegative. A maximization is the same geometry only after the cost is replaced by its negative, so leaving the word maximize does not match the form. Inequalities are not yet equalities, and a free variable is not yet a nonnegative variable. Both of those are rewritten before the form is standard.

questions.prompt: A loader minimizes \(5x - 2y\) subject to \(x + y \le 9\) and \(2x + y \ge 4\), with \(x\) free and \(y \ge 0\). How many nonnegative variables does the standard form use?
questions.explanation: The free variable splits as \(x = u - v\) with \(u, v \ge 0\). The upper bound takes one slack and the lower bound takes one surplus. Together with \(y\), that is five nonnegative variables: \(u\), \(v\), \(y\), the slack, and the surplus. Reporting 2 counts only the original names. Reporting 3 forgets the slack and the surplus. Reporting 4 drops either the split or one of the inequality variables.

questions.prompt: A variable that is allowed to be positive or negative is brought into standard form by
questions.explanation: The difference of two nonnegative variables can represent any real number, and both new variables fit the nonnegative requirement. The absolute value is not linear, so dropping it into the cost leaves the program. A slack converts an inequality; it does not remove the freedom of a variable. Squaring produces a quadratic constraint or cost, which is no longer a linear program.

options: writing it as \(u - v\) with \(u \ge 0\) and \(v \ge 0\)
replacing it by its absolute value inside the cost
adding a slack and leaving the variable free
squaring it so the model stays linear

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order of one conversion into standard form. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The sense of the optimization is fixed first, because the standard form is a minimization. Upper bounds are converted next, and the following step refers to those converted bounds, so it cannot come earlier. Lower bounds are then converted by a surplus. Only after every constraint is an equality does the procedure split free variables, because that step is stated to act on the resulting equalities. Splitting a variable before the inequalities are written changes names in constraints that are about to be rewritten anyway, and this procedure does that rewrite first.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 200" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a segment in the first quadrant</title><line x1="40" y1="168" x2="250" y2="168"/><polygon points="250,168 243.6,170.7 243.6,165.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="48" y1="184" x2="48" y2="22"/><polygon points="48,22 50.7,28.4 45.3,28.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="244" y="184" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="56" y="18" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="188" y1="168" x2="48" y2="48" stroke-width="2.4"/><circle cx="188" cy="168" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="48" cy="48" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A segment joining two marked points on the axes.
steps: Replace a maximization by minimizing the negative of the objective, before changing any constraint.
With the objective now a minimization, add a nonnegative slack to each remaining upper-bound inequality.
With those upper bounds converted, subtract a nonnegative surplus from each remaining lower-bound inequality.
With every constraint now an equality, replace each free variable by a difference of two nonnegative variables.

questions.prompt: Which of these programs are already in standard form?
questions.explanation:
Standard form is a minimization, with every constraint an equality and every variable nonnegative. The first program and the last program match that list.
• A maximization is not standard until the cost is negated.
• An inequality is not an equality until a slack or a surplus is introduced.
• A free variable is not nonnegative until it is split.

questions.prompt: The inequality \(\lvert 2x - y \rvert \le 6\) is equivalent to which linear description?
questions.explanation: The absolute value is at most 6 exactly when the expression sits between \(-6\) and \(6\). Those two linear inequalities are the standard-form material: each then receives its own slack. Forcing equality keeps only the upper endpoint. One inequality leaves the lower side open, so \(2x - y = -7\) would still look acceptable. The squared form is equivalent as a set, and it is not linear.

questions.prompt: A note converts \(\min -x + 3y\) subject to \(x + 2y \le 8\), \(x - y \ge 1\), with \(x\) free and \(y \ge 0\). Exactly one step is false. The split is \(x = u - v\).
questions.explanation: Negating the split gives \(-x = -(u - v) = -u + v\), so the objective line is right. An upper bound gains a slack, and the sign in front of \(s\) is right. Every new variable in this conversion is nonnegative, including both pieces of \(x\). The false step is the lower bound. A surplus is subtracted, so the equality is \(u - v - y - t = 1\). Writing \(+ t\) lets \(t\) push the left side up and encodes the wrong direction.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a segment</title><line x1="28" y1="150" x2="256" y2="150"/><polygon points="256,150 249.6,152.7 249.6,147.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="40" y1="164" x2="40" y2="20"/><polygon points="40,20 42.7,26.4 37.3,26.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="166" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="48" y="16" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="36" y1="132" x2="244" y2="36" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="70" y1="112" x2="190" y2="52" stroke-width="2.4"/><circle cx="70" cy="112" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="190" cy="52" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A solid segment joins two marked points on a dashed line.
steps: The upper bound becomes \(u - v + 2y + s = 8\) with \(s \ge 0\).
The lower bound becomes \(u - v - y + t = 1\) with \(t \ge 0\).
The variables \(u, v, y, s, t\) are all required to be nonnegative.
reasons: A surplus is subtracted, so the lower bound is \(u - v - y - t = 1\).
The objective sign on \(v\) is the part that is wrong.
The slack on the upper bound should have been subtracted.

questions.prompt: The inequality \(4x + y \le 11\) is written with a slack. At \((x, y) = (1, 3)\), what is that slack?
questions.explanation: The slack is the unused room \(11 - 4x - y\). At the given point, \(4 \cdot 1 + 3 = 7\), so the slack is \(11 - 7 = 4\). Reporting 7 gives the left-hand side, which is data of the point, not the slack. Reporting 11 gives the right-hand side. Reporting 1 gives a coordinate.

questions.prompt: An inequality \(a x + b y \le p\) is written with a slack. Using the names \(a, x, b, y, p\), that slack equals
questions.explanation: The slack is defined by moving the left-hand side to the other side of the inequality: it equals \(p - a x - b y\), and the equality form is \(a x + b y + s = p\). On the declared ranges the slack stays positive, which is the feasible side of this one inequality. Subtracting \(p\) instead, or adding the left-hand side to \(p\), measures the wrong gap. Leaving out one term forgets part of the linear form.

questions.prompt: Maximize \(x + 2y\) subject to \(x + y \le 5\) and \(x, y \ge 0\). Which system is the standard form?
questions.explanation: The maximization becomes the minimization of \(-x - 2y\). The upper bound receives a slack, so the equality is \(x + y + s = 5\), and \(x, y, s \ge 0\). Keeping the original cost minimizes the wrong direction. A minus in front of the slack is a surplus and encodes \(x + y \ge 5\). Leaving the word maximize means the form is not standard, even though the slack equation is right.

options: Minimize \(x + 2y\) subject to \(x + y + s = 5\), all variables nonnegative.
Minimize \(-x - 2y\) subject to \(x + y + s = 5\), all variables nonnegative.
Minimize \(-x - 2y\) subject to \(x + y - s = 5\), all variables nonnegative.
Maximize \(x + 2y\) subject to \(x + y + s = 5\), all variables nonnegative.

questions.prompt: Maximizing \(6x + y\) is rewritten as a minimization of \(-6x - y\). At \((x, y) = (2, 3)\), what is that standard-form objective?
questions.explanation: The original objective at the point is \(6 \cdot 2 + 3 = 15\). Standard form minimizes the negative, so the value is \(-15\). Reporting 15 keeps the maximization's number. Reporting 12 or 3 reports a product or a coordinate, not the rewritten objective. The feasible set is not involved: the objective value is a property of the point.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: One inequality of a linear program receives, in the conversion to standard form,
questions.explanation: An upper bound is an equality plus one slack. A lower bound is an equality minus one surplus. Using both on the same inequality adds a redundant degree of freedom and is not the conversion. Leaving the inequality as it stands is a general form, not standard form. A free-variable split is for a variable, not for an inequality.
